sections.gastroparesis_overview:
Gastroparesis is a disorder characterized by ‘slow, heavy digestion.’ The condition affects the muscles of the stomach, and hampers the stomach’s ability to digest food. In this condition, the stomach cannot empty itself of the food in a normal manner. 

 The occurrence of Gastroparesis is linked to damage to the ‘vagus’ nerve. This nerve controls the muscles of the stomach and regulates the digestive system by propelling food through the digestive tract, by muscular contractions. The vagus nerve performs a crucial role in managing the complex digestive process. It signals the muscles in the stomach to contract, so that the food is pushed into the small intestine. 
 Due to the damaged vagus nerve in patients suffering from Gastroparesis, the stomach’s muscles cannot function properly, and the spontaneous movement (motility) of the muscles is affected. As such, the stomach is not able to empty itself properly, and the food remains in the stomach a bit longer, instead of getting digested after its normal movement into the small intestine, thus creating wastage. 
 The vagus nerve damage, which leads to Gastroparesis can be caused by certain diseases, like Diabetes, or because of a surgical procedure involving the stomach or small intestine. 
 Gastroparesis can trigger a number of health complications including severe dehydration, hardening of undigested food that remains in the stomach, and frequent changes in blood sugar levels. The disease can, therefore, have an adverse impact on a patient’s quality of life. 
 Gastroparesis can affect both men and women, though it is more likely to develop in women as compared to men.
sections.gastroparesis_causes:
The main cause behind the occurrence of Gastroparesis is the damaged vagus nerve. In addition to this cause, the condition can develop due to some other reasons as well. These reasons may include: 

 Uncontrolled Diabetes 
 Viral infections 
 Gastric (abdominal) surgery that injures the vagus nerve 
 Certain medications, like narcotics and some antidepressants 
 Multiple sclerosis 
 Parkinson’s disease 
 Rare disorders, such as Amyloidosis and Scleroderma.
sections.the_most_common_signs_and_symptoms_of_ga:
Heartburn 
 Acid reflux 
 Abdominal pain 
 Bloating 
 Vomiting undigested food 
 Nausea 
 Feeling of fullness after eating a few bites 
 Poor appetite 
 Weight loss and malnutrition 

 Gastroparesis and Ayurveda 
 As per classical Ayurvedic texts, a ‘slow digestion’ condition like Gastroparesis is a result of the aggravation of one or more of the three doshas of the body — Vata dosha, Pitta dosha, and Kapha dosha. 
 Therefore, Ayurvedic experts advise Gastroparesis patients to avoid the intake of foods, which aggravate the related dosha. 
 In general, Gastroparesis patients should avoid oily, heavy, toxic, sweet, and cold foods. They are advised to eat foods which have clear, pungent and bitter qualities (guna). Moreover, Gastroparesis patients should eat pureed and well-cooked food, chew the food properly, and drink plenty of water.
